title: Cost
description: Class 11 Economics: cost concepts, fixed and variable cost, total cost, average fixed/variable/total cost and marginal cost with a worked table, and the shapes of the cost curves.

topics.title: Cost Concepts: Fixed, Variable and Total Cost
topics.concept:
To produce goods, a firm must pay for its inputs — these payments are its cost of production. A few cost concepts are important. Money cost is the actual money spent; real cost is the effort and sacrifice involved; and opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up (which we met earlier). Here we focus on the money costs of a firm in the short run, where some factors are fixed.

Short-run costs are divided into two kinds:

  • Total Fixed Cost (TFC) — costs that do not change with the level of output. They must be paid even if output is zero (e.g. rent of the factory, salary of permanent staff, insurance). TFC is constant at all levels of output.
  • Total Variable Cost (TVC) — costs that change with the level of output. They are zero when output is zero and rise as output rises (e.g. cost of raw materials, wages of casual workers, power).

The sum of the two is the Total Cost (TC):

TC = TFC + TVC

Since TFC is constant, the shape of the TC curve follows the TVC curve, just raised up by the fixed amount. At zero output, TC equals TFC (because TVC is zero). As output rises, TC rises because TVC rises. Understanding the split between fixed and variable cost is the foundation for all the average and marginal cost ideas that follow.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the difference between fixed cost and variable cost?
examples.solution:
One changes with output, one does not.

  • Fixed cost (TFC) does not change with output and must be paid even at zero output (e.g. rent).
  • Variable cost (TVC) changes with output and is zero at zero output (e.g. raw materials).
examples.answer: Fixed cost stays the same at all output levels (e.g. rent); variable cost changes with output (e.g. raw materials).

examples.problem: Example 2: If TFC = ₹500 and TVC = ₹700, find total cost.
Example 3: What does total cost equal when output is zero, and why?
examples.solution:
At zero output TVC is zero.

  • TC = TFC + TVC = TFC + 0 = TFC.
  • Fixed cost must still be paid even with no output.
examples.answer: TC equals TFC at zero output, because TVC is zero but fixed cost still has to be paid.

recap:
• Cost concepts: money cost, real cost, opportunity cost.
  • TFC = fixed cost (constant, paid even at zero output — rent); TVC = variable cost (changes with output, zero at zero output — raw materials).
  • TC = TFC + TVC; at zero output TC = TFC.

quiz.q: Which cost must be paid even when output is zero?
quiz.explanation: Fixed cost (TFC) is paid regardless of output.

topics.title: Average and Marginal Cost
topics.concept:
From total costs we derive the per-unit and extra-unit costs that a firm watches most closely:

  • Average Fixed Cost (AFC) = TFC ÷ Q. As output rises, the same fixed cost is spread over more units, so AFC continuously falls.
  • Average Variable Cost (AVC) = TVC ÷ Q. AVC first falls, reaches a minimum, then rises (U-shaped).
  • Average Total Cost (AC or ATC) = TC ÷ Q = AFC + AVC. AC is also U-shaped.
  • Marginal Cost (MC) = the addition to total cost when one more unit is produced = change in TC (or change in TVC), MC = TCₙ − TCₙ₋₁. MC is U-shaped too.

Notice AFC keeps falling, AVC and AC dip then rise, and MC = the change in TC. A key link: AC = AFC + AVC, and MC cuts both AVC and AC at their lowest points.

examples.problem: Example 1: Write the formulas for AFC, AVC, AC and MC.
examples.solution:
Averages divide by Q; MC is the change in TC.

  • AFC = TFC ÷ Q; AVC = TVC ÷ Q; AC = TC ÷ Q.
  • MC = change in TC (TCₙ − TCₙ₋₁).
examples.answer: AFC = TFC ÷ Q, AVC = TVC ÷ Q, AC = TC ÷ Q, and MC = change in TC.

examples.problem: Example 2: From the table, find the MC of the 4th unit.
Example 3: Why does AFC fall continuously as output rises?
examples.solution:
Fixed cost is spread thinner.

  • TFC is constant; dividing it by a larger Q gives a smaller value each time.
examples.answer: Because the constant fixed cost is spread over more and more units, so TFC ÷ Q keeps falling.

recap:
• AFC = TFC÷Q (falls continuously); AVC = TVC÷Q (U-shaped); AC = TC÷Q = AFC + AVC (U-shaped); MC = change in TC (U-shaped).
  • MC cuts AVC and AC at their minimum points.

quiz.q: Average fixed cost (AFC) as output rises:
quiz.explanation: Fixed cost spread over more units means AFC falls continuously.

options: Change in total cost from one more unit
quiz.explanation: MC is the addition to total cost from producing one more unit.

topics.title: Shapes of the Cost Curves
topics.concept:
Plotting the cost figures gives the famous family of cost curves, whose shapes you must know:

  • The AFC curve falls continuously and gets closer and closer to the X-axis but never touches it (it is a rectangular hyperbola), because fixed cost is spread over more units.
  • The AVC curve is U-shaped — it falls, reaches a minimum, then rises (because of the law of variable proportions acting in reverse on costs).
  • The AC (ATC) curve is also U-shaped and lies above the AVC curve; the gap between them is the AFC, which narrows as output rises.
  • The MC curve is U-shaped too, and it cuts both the AVC and AC curves at their lowest (minimum) points from below.

These relationships are shown below:

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the shape of the AFC curve, and why?
examples.solution:
It falls but never reaches zero.

  • It falls continuously (a rectangular hyperbola) approaching the X-axis.
  • Because fixed cost is spread over more units, but never becomes zero.
examples.answer: The AFC curve falls continuously (a rectangular hyperbola), getting closer to the X-axis but never touching it.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why are the AVC, AC and MC curves U-shaped?
examples.solution:
Costs fall then rise.

  • Each first falls, reaches a minimum, then rises (due to the law of variable proportions acting on costs).
examples.answer: Because each cost first falls, reaches a minimum, then rises (the cost side of the law of variable proportions) — giving a U shape.

examples.problem: Example 3: Where does the MC curve cut the AVC and AC curves?
examples.solution:
At their lowest points.

  • MC cuts both AVC and AC at their minimum points from below.
examples.answer: At their minimum (lowest) points, cutting them from below.

recap:
• AFC: falls continuously (rectangular hyperbola), never zero.
  • AVC, AC, MC: all U-shaped; AC lies above AVC (gap = AFC, narrowing).
  • MC cuts AVC and AC at their minimum points from below.

quiz.q: The AFC curve is shaped like a:
quiz.explanation: AFC falls continuously as a rectangular hyperbola.

quiz.q: The MC curve cuts the AC curve at AC's:
quiz.explanation: MC intersects AC at AC's minimum point.

questions.q: The value of the next-best alternative foregone is the ____ cost.
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative given up.

questions.q: Costs that do not change with output are:
questions.explanation: Fixed costs (TFC) do not change with output.

questions.q: Costs that change with the level of output are:
questions.explanation: Variable costs (TVC) change with output.

questions.q: Total cost equals:
questions.explanation: TC = TFC + TVC.

questions.q: At zero output, total cost equals:
questions.explanation: TC = TFC at zero output (TVC is zero).

questions.q: Average fixed cost is:
questions.explanation: AFC = TFC ÷ Q.

questions.q: As output rises, AFC:
questions.explanation: AFC falls continuously as fixed cost is spread thinner.

questions.q: Average total cost equals:
questions.explanation: AC = AFC + AVC (= TC ÷ Q).

questions.q: Marginal cost is the:
options: Change in total cost from one more unit
questions.explanation: MC = change in total cost when one more unit is produced.

questions.q: If TC rises from 27 to 36 when output rises from 3 to 4, MC is:
The AVC curve is:
questions.explanation: AVC is U-shaped (falls then rises).

questions.q: The AFC curve is a:
questions.explanation: AFC continuously falls as a rectangular hyperbola.

questions.q: The MC curve cuts the AVC and AC curves at their:
questions.explanation: MC cuts AVC and AC at their minimum points.

questions.q: The vertical gap between the AC and AVC curves equals the:
questions.explanation: AC − AVC = AFC, which is the gap between the curves.

questions.q: Rent of a factory building is an example of a ____ cost.
questions.explanation: Factory rent does not vary with output — a fixed cost.

questions.q: A bakery pays ₹2,000 rent whether it bakes 0 or 100 loaves. This ₹2,000 is a:
questions.explanation: Rent does not change with output, so it is a fixed cost.

questions.q: If TFC = ₹100 and at 10 units TVC = ₹150, then AC at 10 units is:
AFC keeps falling but never reaches zero because total fixed cost:
options: Stays positive while being spread over more units
questions.explanation: A constant positive TFC divided by an ever-larger Q approaches, but never reaches, zero.

questions.q: When MC is below AC, the AC curve is:
questions.explanation: While MC lies below AC it pulls AC down, so AC falls — until MC = AC at AC's minimum.

questions.q: The gap between the AC and AVC curves narrows as output rises because:
questions.explanation: AC − AVC = AFC, and AFC declines with output, so the two curves draw closer.

questions.q: Why are the AVC and AC curves U-shaped?
options: First increasing then diminishing returns make per-unit costs fall then rise
questions.explanation: The law of variable proportions makes costs per unit fall in the efficient range and rise as returns diminish.

questions.q: A firm shut for the day still pays its watchman and rent. These payments confirm that fixed costs:
options: Must be borne even at zero output
questions.explanation: Fixed costs continue regardless of output, even when nothing is produced.

questions.q: Using the table, the AVC is lowest (₹5) and then begins to rise around output:
questions.explanation: AVC = 5 at Q = 2 and 3, then rises to 6 and 8 — its minimum is around 2–3 units.

questions.q: Marginal cost is closely linked to total variable cost because MC equals the change in:
options: TVC (the only part of TC that changes with output)
questions.explanation: Since TFC is constant, any change in TC comes from TVC, so MC = ΔTC = ΔTVC.

questions.q: At AC's minimum point, marginal cost is:
questions.explanation: The MC curve passes through the lowest point of AC, so there MC = AC.
